text: A few weeks ago, I asked my\h audience some odd questions, and more than 13,000 people answered.
Some folks tried to work out what\h the video was going to be about, but very few guessed correctly,
and that's because they didn't\h have the other piece of the puzzle:
I also paid a professional polling service\h to ask the same questions to the public.
What I was actually trying to\h answer is: How Weird Is My Audience?
There’s a deliberate\h double-meaning to "weird" there. If I poll people watching this channel,
the results will have the same bias that plagues\h psychology experiments: you're WEIRD.
Western, Educated, and from Industrialised, Rich and Democratic countries.
Not all of you, not as individuals, but overall, that's what viewers here tend to be.
That WEIRD bias is why many psychology\h experiments that talk about “humans”\h\h
are actually just talking about college\h students from America. But because of that,
I didn’t compare this\h audience to the entire world. That would have been very expensive,
involve translating questions into many languages, and it wouldn’t actually have been that\h meaningful to most people watching.
Instead, the polling service asked that I pick one\h English-speaking country to compare against.
Most of my viewers are American, and the US was also the cheapest to poll, so,
we are comparing my audience to a representative\h sample of just over 1500 adults from the US.
For some questions, I expected to\h find a big difference.
For some, I expected no difference at all.\h And for some questions… well,
I just found them funny. Question one!

The internet likes cats, I guess.
Next question. I put a call out for academics\h who were looking for a large audience to poll,
and while only one of those questions actually\h made it into the survey, I really do find it fascinating.
This came from researchers at the School of\h Advanced Study at the University of London,

aphantasiacs are people who don’t have a mind’s eye, but that’s already been polled a lot:
this is asking whether you have a mind’s nose. It took a while to hammer out\h the question into a form that’d\h\h
work for the polling company. So it’s not perfect --
it does exclude folks who can imagine smells\h but can’t imagine pictures or sounds,
but that should just be a\h very small number of people.
Here are the results from the\h public. And they’re puzzling,
because they do not match what\h the researchers expected at all.
About a quarter of folks said that they can’t imagine\h\h a loved one’s face or play back a\h familiar song in their head.
Now, aphantasia like that is a thing, absolutely,
but it’s meant to affect only a small\h percentage of people, probably less than 5%,
so that indicates the question\h might have gone wrong somewhere.
The results from my audience, meanwhile...
they're more or less what the researchers\h expected. That makes a lot more sense.
The most likely explanation, I think, is that it’s a complicated\h question. It requires thought,
and the public who were being\hasked, well, they're being paid to answer.
A significant number of\hpeople won’t think about the question, and will pick whichever answer will get them\h\h
through the survey as fast\h as possible. So in this case,
I’d trust my audience to be more\h representative of the world at large,
just because there’s no profit\h motive there. So in this case: my guess is that you’re normal.
Now, when I put the call out for questions, there were a lot of divisive\h but meaningless ones suggested.
Whether the toilet paper should go over or under. Whether the centre or the edge of the\h brownie is better. But no-one suggested:
should you put one or two spaces after a period, or a full stop if you’re British.
And that’s the reason I went for the question. Because it is divisive out there in the world,
but no-one in my audience thought to ask about it. HTML, the language that the web\h is built on, collapses whitespace.
In the code that makes up web sites, it doesn’t matter if you use\h one, or two, or fifty spaces,
they all get crushed down to one\h unless you specifically tell it not to.
And a lot of sites don’t\h bother doing that. So often, even if you do type two spaces after a period,
it’ll appear as one to whoever’s reading it. I’m not going to weigh in on the argument myself,
because it could be a whole video on\h its own, but I will say this: wow,
does my audience disagree with the world here.
The public are almost split down\h the middle. 55% say “one space”,
45% say two. If you break it down by age, there is a trend towards one space,
but even among 18-24 year olds,\h it’s still only about 70-30.
My audience? 95% one-spacers.\h Even for people over 65,
more than three-quarters just use one space. And my theory on this is simple:
most of the audience for\h this poll came from Twitter. I did try to post it on my\h YouTube community tab as well,
and y’all crashed Google Forms by rushing to it. So that’s a new responsibility I have to\h worry about. But even allowing for that,
one space is the standard on\h basically every social media site. If you do post with two spaces after a period,
it’s now a pretty big sign that\h you’re not used to the internet.
And my audience tend to be used to the internet. So congratulations to the one-spacers.

Were they trying to appear more in-touch than\h they actually were? I wouldn’t like to guess.

Which brings us to the final question. How weird do you think you are?
No guidance. No examples.\h Just a scale to pick from: “very normal” to “very weird”.
And this… I think this was the\h most revealing difference of all. Because for the general public,
there’s quite a spread of opinion. 7% are happy thinking of\h themselves as “very normal”.
14% think of themselves as “very weird”. Around half sit in the middle.
Women tend to rate themselves slightly more weird;\h\h older folks tend to rate themselves\h slightly less weird. That’s the public.
But for this audience…
Almost no-one wants to think of themselves as\h being “very normal”. Less than half a percent.
And under 5% think of themselves as “very weird”.
More than 40% described themselves as slightly\h more weird than average. Don’t get me wrong,
that’s still the majority\hopinion of the public as well,
it turns out most people like to think they’re\h just a little bit out there compared to the world,
but the people in this audience are much, much less likely to think of themselves as being\h\h
on the extreme ends of the\hscale, in either direction.
Is that because you’re more likely to be\h spending lots of time on the internet, to have been exposed to more people and opinions,
and therefore have a different boundary\h for what “normal” and “weird” mean?\h\h
Is it because, ironically, you are more likely to conform,
and to want to sit\hin the middle of the chart and not draw attention to yourself?
Or is it just that the public,\h when paid to answer a survey, don’t think it through?
I\hdon’t know the reason why. But big picture: the answer to “how\hweird is my audience”?
Probably, more weird than you think you are.
